prompt: On a freshly started boxoffice, an order for 4 seats of sh-101 is accepted. What total_cents should its body carry?
hint: Lesson 1. Look up the price of sh-101.

prompt: A server answers 200 with `content-type: text/plain`, and the body is JSON with every field right. What does a tester conclude?
hint: Lesson 1. What does a client read before the body?

choices.text: No defect: the fields are right, and those are what a test checks
choices.why: The label decides how the body is read; a right body under a wrong label is unusable.

choices.text: Fine, since the status code says it worked
choices.why: The status code comes first, and the label is the next thing checked.

choices.text: A defect in curl, which picked the label when it received the answer
choices.why: curl prints the label the server sent; it does not choose one.

choices.text: A defect: a client that trusts the label will not parse it
choices.why: Right. The headers that describe the body come before the body in what a tester reads.

prompt: A colleague's test looks for a response header spelt exactly `Content-Type` and fails against boxoffice, which sends `content-type`. Where is the defect?
hint: Lesson 1, the section on headers.

choices.text: In boxoffice: header names should be capitalised the way curl writes them
choices.why: curl's capitals are a habit, not a rule; HTTP/2 even requires lower case.

choices.text: In neither: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 disagree, so the check should be dropped
choices.why: They agree that names are case-insensitive; the check is worth keeping, written correctly.

choices.text: In the test: header names are not case-sensitive
choices.why: Right. Content-Type and content-type are one header, and a test comparing them letter for letter has a defect of its own.

choices.text: In boxoffice: it should copy the request's case
choices.why: Nothing ties the case of a response to the case of a request; neither carries meaning.

prompt: A method that changes nothing on the server, so that a client, a cache or a test may send it as often as it likes, is called ___.
hint: Lesson 1. GET and HEAD are; POST is not.

prompt: Another API answers `DELETE /v1/shows/sh-101`, a show that exists and cannot be deleted, with 404. What should the report ask for?
hint: Lesson 1. What does 404 claim about the address?

choices.text: Nothing: any 4xx tells the client not to send it again
choices.why: The class is right and the code is not; 404 claims the show is absent, which is false.

choices.text: A 400, because a DELETE to a show is a malformed request
choices.why: The request is well formed; it asks for something the address does not offer.

choices.text: A 403, since nobody may delete a show
choices.why: 403 is about who is asking; here the verb is refused for every caller, which is 405.

choices.text: A 405 with an allow header listing what the address accepts
choices.why: Right. The address exists and the method is not accepted there, which is what 405 says.

prompt: On a freshly started boxoffice, a valid token orders 5 seats of sh-103. What comes back?
hint: Lesson 2. Which rule does 5 break, the contract's or the show's?

choices.text: 422, because 5 seats is outside the rule for an order
choices.why: The rule is 1 to 6, and 5 is inside it.

choices.text: 201 for 4 seats, the most the show still has
choices.why: boxoffice never changes the quantity it was asked for; it refuses or accepts the order as sent.

choices.text: 409, only 4 seats left
choices.why: Right. The body is valid; the state of the server forbids it, which is what 409 says.

choices.text: 400, because the body cannot be read as an order
choices.why: The body is valid JSON and a valid order; 400 is for a body that cannot be read.

prompt: An app wants to tell the user apart "sold out" and "choose between 1 and 6 seats" when an order to boxoffice is refused. What should its code decide on?
hint: Lesson 2, problem details. boxoffice's type is about:blank everywhere.

choices.text: The wording of detail, which differs between the two refusals
choices.why: detail is written for people, and somebody will one day reword it.

choices.text: The status code, 409 against 422
choices.why: Right. With type always about:blank, the status code is what a program has to branch on.

choices.text: The type field, which names each kind of problem
choices.why: In boxoffice it is about:blank for every error, so it tells the two apart in no case.

choices.text: The content-type header
choices.why: Both errors are application/problem+json.

prompt: Which of these answers to `POST /v1/orders` would break the contract in openapi.yaml, whatever their body said?
hint: Lesson 2. The contract lists the codes the operation may give.

choices.why: Right. It is not in the list, so the client was told it would never see one.
Listed: a declined payment.
Right. The operation lists 502 and 504, not 503.
Listed: the payment provider did not answer in time.
Right. An unknown show is a 422 here; 404 is not among the operation's codes.

prompt: A report adds prices in reais as JavaScript numbers. A test buys three tickets at R$ 80,10 and checks `total === 240.3`. What happens?
hint: Lesson 2, money.

choices.text: It passes, because 80.10 has two decimal places and so does the total
choices.why: Two decimals in the text are not two decimals in binary floating point.

choices.text: It fails, because the sum comes out as 240.29999999999998
choices.why: Right. Node printed exactly that; the same sum in cents is exactly 24030.

choices.text: It fails, because JSON has no way to carry a number with decimals
choices.why: JSON carries 80.10 perfectly well; the error comes from adding it as binary floating point.

choices.text: It passes: JavaScript rounds to the cent
choices.why: JavaScript does no such rounding; the screen does, which is why the error hides there.

prompt: In openapi.yaml a path does not repeat the shape of an order; it points at `NewOrder` in components with the keyword ___.
hint: Lesson 2. It starts with a dollar sign.

prompt: A new staff API answers a request with no key with "key missing" and a request with a wrong key with "key not recognised", both as 401. What do you report?
hint: Lesson 3, the staff key.

choices.text: Nothing: the two messages help the client's author find the mistake
choices.why: They help a stranger too, by saying which requests came close to being right.

choices.text: That the wrong key should get 403, because the server knows a key was sent
choices.why: A key the server does not hold identifies nobody, so 401 is the right code; the messages are the issue.

choices.text: That both refusals should read the same, word for word
choices.why: Right. boxoffice answers both alike, and that sameness is what keeps a stranger's guesses blind.

choices.text: That the key should travel in the query string so the server logs which one failed
choices.why: An address is logged by default, so that would put the key in the log; the lesson tests that it is refused there.

prompt: Match each claim in a boxoffice token's payload to what it holds.
hint: Lesson 3, inside a JWT.

pairs.right: the client the token is about
what the token may do, separated by spaces
when it was issued, in seconds since 1970
when it stops working, in the same seconds

right_distractors: the secret it was signed with

prompt: boxoffice runs with `TOKEN_TTL=5`, and a token's payload says `"iat":1791661400`. What number does its exp claim hold?
hint: Lesson 3. exp is iat plus the lifetime in seconds.

prompt: Testing another API, you send a token whose header says `"alg":"none"` and whose signature is empty, and it creates an order with 201. What is your verdict?
hint: Lesson 3. Who can make such a token?

choices.text: Acceptable, since the claims inside the token were valid
choices.why: Without a checked signature the claims are whatever the sender typed.

choices.text: A serious defect: any client could grant itself any scope
choices.why: Right. A server that skips the signature accepts tokens nobody signed, which is the edited-token test failing.

choices.text: A minor defect: it should have answered 403 rather than 201
choices.why: The problem is not which refusal; the token should not have been accepted as anybody at all, which is a 401.

choices.text: Expected, because a JWT is encrypted and alg just names the cipher
choices.why: A JWT is signed, not encrypted; alg names how it was signed.

prompt: Put the steps of the authorization code flow with PKCE in order.
hint: Lesson 3. The verifier travels last.
items: the app makes a verifier and computes its challenge
the app opens the browser with its client id, state and challenge
the person signs in on the authorization server's page
the browser returns to the app with a code and the same state
the app sends the code and the verifier to the token endpoint
the server hashes the verifier, compares, and answers with a token

prompt: A team keeps one boxoffice collection and two environments, lab and staging. Which of these belong in the environments rather than in the collection?
hint: Lesson 4. What changes from one server to another?

choices.text: baseUrl
choices.why: Right. The address is the first thing that differs between servers.

choices.text: clientSecret
choices.why: Right. Credentials differ per server, and the shared file should leave the real one empty.

choices.text: showId, the show the requests order from
choices.why: It belongs to this API's requests, which is what collection variables are for.

choices.text: the bearer authorization the folders inherit
choices.why: Authorization is set on the collection and its folders; only the token's value is a variable.

choices.text: clientId
choices.why: Right. Another server may have its own client for the tests.

prompt: You import an environment a teammate exported. In their Postman clientSecret shows a value, and in yours it is empty. What explains it?
hint: Lesson 4. Postman keeps two values for each variable.

choices.text: The import failed on a missing comma and dropped that value
choices.why: A broken file fails to import at all; jq would name the line.

choices.text: The secret type encrypts the value inside the exported file
choices.why: secret only hides a value on the screen; a file that carries it carries it in plain text.

choices.text: Their value was the local one, which stays on their computer
choices.why: Right. An exported file carries only the shared value, and theirs was kept local.

choices.text: A global variable called clientSecret in your workspace is hiding it
choices.why: A global is the widest scope; the environment would win over it, not the other way round.

prompt: You add a folder called reports to lesson 4's collection, with no auth entry, and in it a GET to /v1/reports/sales with no other header. What does boxoffice answer?
hint: Lesson 4 for what the folder inherits, lesson 3 for what the report wants.

choices.text: 200, because the folder inherits the collection's credentials
choices.why: It inherits the bearer token, and the report does not accept a token.

choices.text: 403, because ci-tests has no scope for reports
choices.why: The report never reads a token's scope; it refuses anything without the key, as a 401.

choices.text: Postman refuses to send it until the folder names an auth type
choices.why: No auth entry means inherit; nothing stops the request.

choices.text: 401: the bearer token is sent and the staff key is not
choices.why: Right. A folder that says nothing inherits bearer, and the report wants X-Api-Key.

prompt: Put the requests of lesson 4's collection in the order a run of the whole collection sends them.
hint: Lesson 4. Folder by folder, top to bottom.
items: List shows
One show
Get token
Create order
Read order
Cancel order

prompt: A teammate moves the save into the test: `pm.test('status is 201', () => { pm.response.to.have.status(201); pm.collectionVariables.set('orderUrl', pm.response.headers.get('location')); })`. One run, Create order gets 409. What happens to orderUrl?
hint: Lesson 5. Where does a failing assertion stop?

choices.text: It keeps what it held before, so later requests act on an older order
choices.why: Right. The failed assertion stopped the function, and the save after it was skipped exactly when the answer was unusual.

choices.text: It is set to null, since a 409 carries no location
choices.why: The set line never runs: the assertion above it threw first.

choices.text: It is set as usual, because pm.test runs every line before judging
choices.why: pm.test runs the function and fails it at the first throw; nothing after the throw runs.

choices.text: Newman stops the whole run at the failed test
choices.why: Only --bail stops a run; without it Newman goes on to the next request.

prompt: In postman/seats.csv, a row whose seats field must reach the JSON body as the string "2", quotes included, writes that field as ___.
hint: Lesson 5. In CSV a quote inside a quoted field is written twice.

prompt: seats.csv grows to nine data rows. Newman runs only the seat rules folder with it, and the token fetched before the first iteration stays valid. How many requests does the table count?
hint: Lesson 5. Six rows made seven requests.

prompt: A test asserts that the shows list has exactly three entries. It passes today. When does it fail with nothing broken?
hint: Lesson 5, what not to assert.

choices.text: When the theatre adds a show
choices.why: Right. Three is true of boxoffice today and was never promised; assert that there are shows and what each holds.

choices.text: When the run is repeated against the same server without a restart
choices.why: Orders change seats_left, not how many shows there are.

choices.text: On the day after the transcripts were recorded, because of the Date header
choices.why: That was the brittle collection's Date test; this one does not read the date.

choices.text: When a token expires during the run
choices.why: The shows need no token, and the pre-request script renews one anyway.

prompt: A pipeline step is written `run: node boxoffice.mjs > boxoffice.log 2>&1`, without the `&`. What happens to the job?
hint: Lesson 6. Does boxoffice ever exit on its own?

choices.text: Newman runs before the server is ready and the requests are refused
choices.why: Newman never gets to run: the step before it does not end.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because GitHub starts each step in the background
choices.why: A step runs in the foreground until its command exits; that is what the & is for.

choices.text: It stops on that step, waiting, until GitHub kills the job
choices.why: Right. The step waits for a server that never exits, and the collection never runs.

choices.text: boxoffice exits at once because its output goes to a file
choices.why: Sending output to a file does not stop a server; it keeps listening.

prompt: Lesson 6's table counted 11 prerequest-scripts. Somebody removes the pre-request script of Order seats and changes nothing else. How many does the next whole-collection run count?
hint: Lesson 6. The collection's script runs before each of the 9 requests in the file, plus the requests' own.

prompt: A Newman run prints a table whose requests row says 10 executed and 10 failed, and every assertion failed too. What is the first thing to suspect?
hint: Lesson 6. What does the failed column of requests count?

choices.text: boxoffice answered 4xx to every request
choices.why: An error status is an answer; requests that got answers are not counted as failed.

choices.text: The token expired halfway through the run
choices.why: An expired token is answered with 401, which still counts as a request that worked.

choices.text: The tests were written for another version of Newman
choices.why: A test-script problem shows in test-scripts or assertions, not in requests.

choices.text: boxoffice is not running, or the address is wrong
choices.why: Right. That row counts requests that could not be sent at all.

prompt: npm hands a script the arguments of `npm run test:api` that come after a marker of two characters, which is ___.
hint: Lesson 6. Two characters.

prompt: A REST Assured test checks `.body("price_cents", equalTo("6500"))` against sh-103. What happens?
hint: Lesson 7, the matchers.

choices.text: It passes: Hamcrest turns both sides into text before comparing
choices.why: equalTo compares value and type, and does no such conversion.

choices.text: It passes, because JSON has a single kind of number
choices.why: One kind of number, yes, but "6500" in the test is a string, not a number.

choices.text: It fails: the body holds the number 6500, not text
choices.why: Right. equalTo is exact, of that type, and a string is not the number.

choices.text: It does not compile, since Java refuses a string there
choices.why: equalTo takes any type, so it compiles and fails at run time.

prompt: mvn test ends with `Tests run: 11, Failures: 0, Errors: 11`. Where do you look first?
hint: Lesson 7. A failure and an error point at different places.

choices.text: At boxoffice's answers, since eleven checks did not hold
choices.why: A check that did not hold is a failure, and there are none.

choices.text: Nowhere: errors are warnings and the build is green
choices.why: Errors turn the build red just as failures do.

choices.text: At the pom.xml, since Surefire found no tests
choices.why: It found and ran eleven; a missing Surefire pin shows as Tests run: 0.

choices.text: At the lab: whether boxoffice is running where the tests send
choices.why: Right. An error is a test that could not finish, such as a request that threw because nobody answered.

prompt: Lesson 7's suite reported Tests run 11. You add ReportTest.java with two @Test methods and ReportCheck.java with three, both in src/test/java/boxoffice. What does mvn test report now?
hint: Lesson 7. Which class names does Surefire run?

prompt: The REST Assured tests compile in one terminal and fail to compile in another, on the same laptop. What does the lesson point at?
hint: Lesson 7. Read the Java version line of mvn -version.

choices.text: A cache in ~/.m2 that one of the terminals does not see
choices.why: ~/.m2 belongs to the user, and both terminals read the same one.

choices.text: JAVA_HOME pointing at a different JDK in each
choices.why: Right. Maven compiles with the JDK JAVA_HOME names, which need not be the one java -version shows.

choices.text: boxoffice running in only one of them
choices.why: A server that is not running gives errors when the tests run, not a compilation failure.

choices.text: An IDE that compiles behind the terminal's back
choices.why: The lesson needs no IDE; the difference is which JDK Maven uses.

prompt: To run one method of a class, -Dtest takes the class name, then the character ___, then the method name.

pairs.right: the same keys and values, and nothing extra
a holds b among other things
every item of the list a passes b

prompt: A feature's Background says `* header Authorization = 'Bearer ' + ci.token`, and its scenario posts an order and then reads it back with a GET. What happens?
hint: Lesson 8. header against configure headers.

choices.text: The POST carries the token and the GET goes without it, so it gets 401
choices.why: Right. header adds to the next request only; configure headers is what lasts.

choices.text: Both requests carry the token, since the Background runs before the scenario
choices.why: It runs before the scenario, but header applies only to the next request.

choices.text: Neither carries it: header is ignored inside a Background
choices.why: It is not ignored; the first request after it gets the header.

choices.text: Karate refuses the feature, because header needs a Given
choices.why: Given, When, Then and * are interchangeable; Karate refuses nothing here.

prompt: The full Karate run reported 16 tests. Three more rows are added to the Examples of seats.feature, and head.feature is deleted. How many tests does the next full run report?
hint: Lesson 8. Each row of an Outline is a test, and so is each scenario.

prompt: A colleague copies a pom.xml from an older article that names `com.intuit.karate:karate-junit6:2.1.2`. What happens on mvn test?
hint: Lesson 8, the project.

choices.text: It works, because Maven Central redirects the old group to the new one
choices.why: Nothing redirects; a group and an artifact name one entry or nothing.

choices.text: It runs no tests and prints BUILD SUCCESS, as an unpinned Surefire does
choices.why: That is lesson 7's trap; here the dependency itself cannot be found.

choices.text: Maven cannot resolve it: Karate 2 is published under io.karatelabs
choices.why: Right. com.intuit.karate is the group Karate had before it moved, and Karate 2 exists only under the new one.

choices.text: It downloads an older Karate whose feature syntax differs
choices.why: No Karate 2.1.2 exists under the old group to download.

prompt: Match each thing you may see in a SOAP exchange to what it tells a tester.
hint: Lesson 9, the two versions.

prompt: A new version of the invoice WSDL adds `<xs:element name="discountCents" type="xs:positiveInteger" minOccurs="0"/>`. Which request breaks this contract?
hint: Lesson 9, the types part. What does minOccurs="0" change?

choices.text: One that leaves discountCents out
choices.why: minOccurs="0" makes the element optional; without it, an element must appear exactly once.

choices.text: One that sends a discountCents of 0
choices.why: Right. Optional is not untyped: when it is there, it must be a positive integer, and 0 is not.

choices.text: One with a discountCents of 500
choices.why: 500 is a positive integer, which is what the type asks for.

choices.text: Any request that still omits buyerTaxId's 11-digit rule
choices.why: That rule lives in the code, not in the WSDL; the schema calls buyerTaxId a string.

prompt: In a SoapUI test case, the invoiceNumber from one reply must go into the next request. Which test step does that?
hint: Lesson 9, SoapUI described from the outside.

choices.text: A Delay step
choices.why: Delay only waits; it moves no value.

choices.text: A Schema Compliance assertion
choices.why: That is an assertion on one reply, checking it against the WSDL's types; it passes nothing on.

choices.text: A Property Transfer step
choices.why: Right. It copies a value out of one reply into the next request, by XPath.

choices.text: A MockService answering the next request
choices.why: A MockService pretends to be the service; it does not carry values between steps.

prompt: Another tool's validator leaves format checking off unless it is asked. It checks a show whose starts_at is "8/11 18h" against schemas/show.json. What does it say?
hint: Lesson 10. What is format on its own?

choices.text: Valid: it is a string, and format is no more than a note there
choices.why: Right. The standard leaves format checking optional, so the date passes unless the validator is told to check it.

choices.text: Invalid, because a date is not a string in JSON
choices.why: JSON has no date type; a date travels as a string, and this one is a string.

choices.text: Invalid, because starts_at has to match date-time
choices.why: That is what Ajv said with ajv-formats added; with format checking off, nothing reads the keyword.

choices.text: It refuses the schema, because format is a 2020-12 keyword
choices.why: format is old and widely known; the trouble is only whether the validator checks it.

prompt: check.mjs, with the fixed schemas/order.json, is given `{"id":"ord-7","show_id":"sh-101","seats":0,"total_cents":-100,"status":"cancelled","venue":"x"}`. How many lines of broken rules does it print?
hint: Lesson 10. allErrors reports every rule, and a cancelled order needs no payment.

prompt: Which of these changes to boxoffice's show answer would fail the verification of the Tickets app's pact?
hint: Lesson 10. Read the matchingRules, and which fields the pact names.

choices.text: seats_left sent as the string "4"
choices.why: Right. The pact's rule for seats_left is integer.

choices.text: starts_at sent as 2026-11-08T21:00:00Z
choices.why: Right. The regex ends with an offset such as -03:00, and Z does not match it.

choices.text: The play renamed, so title holds another string
choices.why: The title's rule is type: any string will do.

choices.text: price_cents removed from the show
choices.why: The pact never mentions price_cents, because the show screen does not read it.

prompt: A consumer writes a pact with `given('order ord-1001 exists')`, and boxoffice's provider test registers that state with a handler that does nothing. Verification against a freshly started boxoffice fails with a 404. Where is the fix?
hint: Lesson 10. What is a state handler for?

choices.text: In the consumer's test, which should stop naming a state
choices.why: The state is what makes the interaction meaningful; the provider has to be put in it.

choices.text: In the Pact Broker, which should store the order with the pact
choices.why: A broker stores pacts and results; it holds no data for the provider.

choices.text: In boxoffice, which should answer 200 for an order nobody placed
choices.why: A 404 for an order that does not exist is right; the verification ran in the wrong state.

choices.text: In the handler, which should place that order before the interaction
choices.why: Right. A handler readies the provider for its given; sh-103 needed nothing, an order does.

prompt: A teammate testing against the Prism mock of boxoffice gets a show whose title is "string" and files a defect against boxoffice. What do you tell them?
hint: Lesson 11. Where does Prism get its answers?

choices.text: That Prism built it from the schema, which has no example title
choices.why: Right. The shape is right and the content is invented; boxoffice was never asked.

choices.text: That the title field is missing from openapi.yaml
choices.why: It is there, typed as a string; that is exactly why Prism wrote the word string.

choices.text: That boxoffice lost the title when it was restarted
choices.why: Prism never asked boxoffice anything; in mock mode it answers alone.

choices.text: That Prism replays the last answer boxoffice gave it
choices.why: In mock mode Prism forwards nothing and records nothing from boxoffice.

prompt: The approving mapping matches with `"url": "/charges"`. A new boxoffice release posts its charges to /charges?attempt=1. What does WireMock answer?
hint: Lesson 11. url against urlPath.

choices.text: 404, with a report of the closest mapping
choices.why: Right. url matches the path and query exactly; urlPath would ignore the query string.

choices.text: 201 approved, since the path is still /charges
choices.why: That would be true of urlPath; url compares the query string too.

choices.text: 201 declined, from the mapping with priority 1
choices.why: The declining mapping uses url as well, so it does not match either.

choices.text: A 500, the way a provider in trouble answers
choices.why: That is the hand-written stub's down mode, not what WireMock does with an unmatched request.

prompt: With lesson 11's two mapping files loaded, what is the smallest whole amount_cents that WireMock answers as declined?
hint: Lesson 11. Read the filter of charge-declined.json.

prompt: A stand-in that answers as it was told and also records what it received, for the test to read afterwards, is called a ___.
hint: Lesson 11, the vocabulary of stand-ins.

prompt: A fresh boxoffice takes an order for 2 seats of sh-103 and one for 1 seat of sh-101. Once the sales report has caught up, what is its revenue_cents?
hint: Lesson 12. The report sums confirmed orders.

prompt: Two test files both call `start('boxoffice.mjs', { PORT: '8181' })` in before, and node runs them in parallel. What does the second one see?
hint: Lesson 12, tests/start.mjs.

choices.text: Its tests pass against the first file's server, which answers on 8181
choices.why: start waits for its own child to print listening; that child never does.

choices.text: Its tests time out one by one against a dead server
choices.why: That is the failure start.mjs exists to prevent: it rejects when the program exits first.

choices.text: That file fails at once, because its server exits on EADDRINUSE
choices.why: Right. The port is taken, the child exits on EADDRINUSE, and the file fails with that reason.

choices.text: node notices the clash and moves the second server to 8182
choices.why: Nothing moves a port on its own; the second server simply cannot start.

prompt: One morning the report reads `ok 4 - HEAD answers like GET, without a body # TODO boxoffice answers HEAD with 405, lesson 1`. What should you do?

choices.text: Nothing, since the run was already green
choices.why: It was green before too; the ok line says the reason for the todo is gone.

choices.text: Delete the test, since the defect is fixed

choices.text: Change the test to expect 405 again

prompt: Put what happens during a run of tests/payments.test.mjs in order.
hint: Lesson 12. Read the stub's log against the hooks.
items: a token is fetched once
the stub's record is emptied and it is set to approve
an order is placed and the stub's record is read

the stub is set to decline and an order is placed

prompt: A copy of run-integration.sh ends with the grep line and leaves out `exit $status`. One test fails. What does the pipeline show?
hint: Lesson 12. Which command's exit code ends the script then?

choices.text: Red, because node --test exited with 1
choices.why: A script ends with its last command's code, and node --test is not the last.

choices.text: Red, because trap reports the failure when the script ends
choices.why: The trap only kills the servers; it does not change the exit code.

choices.text: Nothing: the script hangs on the servers it started
choices.why: The trap stops both servers whatever happened.

choices.text: Green, because grep found the not ok line
choices.why: Right. grep succeeded, so the script exits 0 and the failure is hidden.

prompt: withRetry runs with its defaults (attempts 4, base 100, cap 2000), a random that always answers 1, and a send that answers 503 every time. How many milliseconds does it wait in all before returning?
hint: Lesson 13. There is no wait after the last attempt.

prompt: Another client allowed to write orders sends the key buy-7f3a, which ci-tests already used for its two-seat order, with the same body. What does it get?
hint: Lesson 13. Whose keys are they?

choices.text: A replay of ci-tests's order, ord-1001
choices.why: That would hand one client another's order; boxoffice keys replies by the token's sub.

choices.text: A new order of its own, with its own id
choices.why: Right. Keys belong to one client, so the same key from another client is a new intention.

choices.text: 422, because the key has already been used
choices.why: 422 is for the same client reusing a key with another body.

choices.text: 409, while ci-tests's order is in progress
choices.why: That is the fix the lesson proposes for the race, and boxoffice does not have it.

prompt: withRetry wraps an order and the first answer is `409 only 1 seat left`. How many times is the order sent?
hint: Lesson 13. Which statuses does RETRYABLE hold?

choices.text: Just once
choices.why: Right. 409 says the state forbids it, so the same request would fail the same way, and RETRYABLE holds only 429, 502, 503 and 504.

choices.text: Four times, the default number of attempts
choices.why: Attempts cap the retries of a retryable answer; a 409 is returned at once.

choices.text: Twice
choices.why: There is no second try, with or without a wait, for a status outside RETRYABLE.

choices.text: Until the seat is free, up to the cap of 2000 ms
choices.why: The cap limits one wait, not the whole loop, and a 409 is not waited on.

prompt: Choosing each wait uniformly between zero and the doubling ceiling, so that clients which failed together spread out, is called full ___.
hint: Lesson 13, waiting between tries.

prompt: An app gets 504 from boxoffice for an order and retries it with the same Idempotency-Key. What happens on boxoffice's side?
hint: Lesson 13. When does boxoffice remember a key?

choices.text: It replays the 504, since the key was already seen
choices.why: boxoffice remembers a key only after a charge succeeds, and this one never did.

choices.text: It places a new order and passes the key to the provider
choices.why: Right. Only a provider that honours idempotency keys can recognise the repeat charge.

choices.text: It answers 422, because the key was used once already
choices.why: 422 is for a key reused with a different body after a remembered reply.

choices.text: It returns the first order, which the timeout had confirmed
choices.why: The first order was marked failed when boxoffice gave up; it confirmed nothing.

prompt: In Tickets, what does price() write for a Show whose priceCents is 6505?
hint: Lesson 14, Shows.kt. The format is "R$ %d,%02d".

choices.why: %02d pads the cents to two digits, so 5 is written 05.
Right. 6505 / 100 is 65, 6505 % 100 is 5, written with two digits.
The remainder is 5 cents, not 50; padding goes on the left.
The integer division by 100 turns cents into reais first.

prompt: Why does Appium name Tickets's button `example.tickets:id/refresh` rather than just `refresh`?
hint: Lesson 14, what the tree looks like.

choices.text: Because Appium adds the package so that XPath can find it faster
choices.why: XPath has nothing to do with it, and the prefix is Android's, not Appium's.

choices.text: Because two apps on one screen each have their own refresh
choices.why: Right. Tickets and the permission dialog drawn over it are different apps, and the package keeps their ids apart.

choices.text: Because the layout file declares the id with the package written in it
choices.why: The layout says @+id/refresh; the package is added by Android when it reports the node.

choices.text: Because a content description must carry a package
choices.why: This is the resource id, not the content description, which has no such prefix.

prompt: Tickets was installed and opened once while boxoffice ran. Then boxoffice is stopped, and the user presses Refresh. What does the list screen show?
hint: Lesson 14, Shows.load and display.

choices.text: The error line and an empty list
choices.why: That is Loaded.Failed, for when nothing was ever saved; the first load saved a copy.

choices.text: The list as it was, with nothing to say it is old
choices.why: display shows the banner whenever the load is Offline.

choices.text: The banner and the error line together
choices.why: display hides both first and shows only one of them per result.

choices.text: The saved list, under the banner Offline: showing the list from HH:mm
choices.why: Right. The request fails, the saved body is parsed, and the banner names the time it was saved.

prompt: Which of these could a local test, running on the computer's own Java runtime without Android, check in Tickets?
hint: Lesson 14, three places a test can live.

choices.text: That price() writes 6500 cents as R$ 65,00
choices.why: Right. Formatting needs no screen, which is what a local test is for.

choices.text: That time() turns the start into 08/11 18:00
choices.why: Right. It is string work, with no Android in it.

choices.text: That tapping a row opens the show's screen
choices.why: That needs the app's views on a device: an instrumented or end-to-end test.

choices.text: That the notification dialog appears when the switch is turned on
choices.why: The dialog belongs to Android; only an end-to-end test sees it.

prompt: Tickets's list screen has no remind switch. Appium's implicit wait is set to 10 seconds, and a test asks whether the switch exists there. What does that cost?
hint: Lesson 15, waiting. Where does an implicit wait act?

choices.text: Nothing: asking about existence is instant
choices.why: With an implicit wait set, every find retries on the server before it answers, this one included.

choices.text: Ten seconds, to prove that something is absent
choices.why: Right. The find retries until the implicit wait runs out, so choose one place to wait: the explicit wait in the test.

choices.text: A failed session, because a find with no match ends it
choices.why: A find with no match answers no such element; the session goes on.

choices.text: Twenty seconds, the time the driver gives adb to find a device
choices.why: That twenty-second wait is for starting a session, not for a find.

hint: Lesson 15, the waits WebdriverIO offers.

prompt: A team wants one Appium locator that finds the Buy button in both the Android and the iOS build of their app. What has to be true of the two builds?
hint: Lesson 15, strategies in order of preference.

choices.text: Both give the button the same resource id, found with the id strategy
choices.why: A resource id is Android's; iOS has no resource ids for the same name to match.

choices.text: Both draw the button at the same place, found by XPath
choices.why: XPath describes positions, and the two platforms build different trees.

choices.text: The same accessibility name in both, found by accessibility id
choices.why: Right. It reads the content description on Android and the accessibility identifier on iOS.

choices.text: Nothing: the UiAutomator strategy works on both platforms
choices.why: UiAutomator exists only on Android.

prompt: `curl localhost:4723/status` answers `"ready": true`. Which of these does that NOT tell you?
hint: Lesson 15, the server.

choices.text: That a device is attached
choices.why: Right. The server learns which device a session is for only when the session asks.

choices.text: That the server is up and accepts sessions
choices.why: That is exactly what ready true says.

choices.text: That Tickets is installed on the emulator
choices.why: Right. The app is installed when a session starts, from appium:app.

choices.text: Which version of Appium is answering
choices.why: The answer carries build.version, 3.8.0.

the Appium server on port 4723

prompt: On the list screen, a test runs `onView(withId(R.id.remind)).check(matches(not(isDisplayed())))`. What happens?
hint: Lesson 16. Is remind ever inflated on the list screen?

choices.text: It fails: no view matches, so NoMatchingViewException
choices.why: Right. remind belongs to the show's screen and was never inflated here, unlike the banner, which exists hidden.

choices.text: It passes, because there is no remind switch to be displayed
choices.why: matches needs a view to judge; with none found, the check never gets that far.

choices.text: It fails with AmbiguousViewMatcherException
choices.why: That is for a matcher that finds more than one view, such as title on the list.

choices.text: It waits until the show's screen opens
choices.why: Espresso waits for the main thread, not for a view to appear.

prompt: A colleague writes `onData(anything()).inAdapterView(withId(R.id.shows)).atPosition(2).perform(click())` to open sh-103. When does it start opening the wrong show?
hint: Lesson 16, why a list needs onData.

choices.text: When the list has been scrolled down before the tap
choices.why: onData scrolls to the item itself; the position is a place in the data, not on the screen.

choices.text: When the emulator is rotated
choices.why: Rotation redraws the screen; the third item of the data is still the third.

choices.text: When boxoffice lists the shows in another order
choices.why: Right. Position finds whatever is third; showWithId("sh-103") finds the show by what the row holds.

choices.text: When sh-103 sells out
choices.why: A sold-out show is still in the list, in the same place.

prompt: A test class registers ShowsIdlingResource in @Before and has no @After. What can that do to the test classes that run after it?
hint: Lesson 16, an idling resource.

choices.text: Nothing: Espresso drops every resource when a class ends
choices.why: IdlingRegistry keeps what it was given until it is told to unregister it.

choices.text: It answers on in their runs, for a finished test
choices.why: Right. Unregistering matters as much as registering, because the registry outlives the class.

choices.text: They stop waiting for the main thread
choices.why: A registered resource adds to what Espresso waits for; it takes nothing away.

choices.text: The app's Shows.busy stays above zero for good
choices.why: The resource only reads busy; it never changes it.

the tests run inside the app's own process

prompt: Which of these does Espresso wait for before each step without being told?
hint: Lesson 16, what Espresso waits for, and what it does not.

choices.text: A new screen being drawn after a tap
choices.why: Right. That is work on the main thread, which Espresso always waits out.

choices.text: The thread Tickets starts to ask boxoffice for the shows
choices.why: A thread the app started itself is invisible to Espresso; that is why the idling resource exists.

choices.text: The pool of background workers that AsyncTask used
choices.why: Right. Espresso watches that pool too, though new code no longer touches it.

choices.text: A list the main thread is still filling
choices.why: Right. Filling the list is main-thread work.

choices.text: A request in flight from another app on the phone
choices.why: Espresso sees only this app's process.

prompt: An Appium test of the React Native list looks for `id=com.ticketsrn:id/refresh` on Android and finds nothing, though the button has testID="refresh". Why?

choices.text: Because a testID becomes a content description, so ~refresh is the locator

choices.text: Because Appium does not see React Native apps, which run in a web view

choices.text: Because testID reaches the iOS build and not Android
choices.why: It reaches both: the resource id on Android, the accessibility identifier on iOS.

prompt: A React Native app is never idle for Detox, and the only cause is a long-lived connection it keeps open to one prices address. The developers cannot change the app this sprint. Which way out keeps the most synchronisation?
hint: Lesson 17, three ways out. What did the blacklist not deal with in the lesson's case?

choices.text: device.disableSynchronization() in beforeAll, for every spec
choices.why: That switches it off for the whole suite, the cost the lesson warns about.

choices.text: A longer Jest timeout, so the wait ends eventually
